"![](images/11/11d38951b884f17616a61403d793322d0e2ea28910e806fe8f018251508352a1.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

- $∇\cdot F=0$
- $∇\cdot F>0$
- $∇\cdot F<0$
- $F$ is solenoidal" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement I is true, whereas statements II and III are false. For any point $P,$ the sum of the inward-pointing vectors equals the sum of the outward-pointing vectors. Therefore, $F$ acts neither like a source nor a sink.

- Statement IV is true. Since $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere, the vector field $F$ is solenoidal.

understanding of what the divergence of a vector field measures.

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ and the point $S,$ shown below. Imagine that this vector field represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. 

![](images/a7/a785c84976242d699af11ab2203600e2007e95e35b60665ba9882c8f0f25bce3.png)

 

We can see from our diagram that $S$ acts like a **source**. You can think of this as an open faucet, pushing water onto the plane and away from itself. 

Since $S$ acts like a source, $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is nonzero. By convention, if a point $S$ acts like a source, the divergence is positive:

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0
$$

In this particular case, *every* point in our vector field acts as a source. So $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0$ everywhere.

If we reverse the situation, we get the following:

![](images/b4/b4c923bbde36568e4e2f36f7d388622a520d0799d558049f72d0194e0bd679f7.png)

 

We can see from our diagram that $T$ acts like a **sink**. You can think of this as an open plughole that sucks in the surrounding water.

Since $T$ acts like a sink, $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is also nonzero. By convention, if a point $T$ acts like a sink, the divergence is negative:

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0
$$

Every point in our vector field acts like a sink in this case. So $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0$ everywhere.

Finally, note that if $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = 0$ everywhere in the domain of some vector field $\mathbf F,$ we say that $\mathbf F$ is **solenoidal.**" :tutorial/id #uuid "a2cdf73b-116c-5cf4-a5a2-a8c95e447127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5518 :tutorial/title "Physical Interpretation of Divergence"} :step/id #uuid "6a9298c4-106a-569c-bd0b-5d24d3e71b0f" :step/math-academy-id 34359 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134848}} {:db/id 17592186134844 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133889 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133705 :question/id #uuid "3cbc5b4a-dde4-59b0-bc34-08c4d8776e0e" :question/math-academy-id "e-9489"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e6b79409-5a5b-533b-8d46-4e0e6d963b3a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134065} {:db/id 17592186134369} {:db/id 17592186235535} {:db/id 17592186259486} {:db/id 17592186259487} {:db/id 17592186259490} {:db/id 17592186266056} {:db/id 17592186266057} {:db/id 17592186266058} {:db/id 17592186362524} {:db/id 17592186383041} {:db/id 17592186385415} {:db/id 17592186407632} {:db/id 17592186424230}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Three Dimensions"} :step/id #uuid "77b5a013-eab6-50c3-9f63-2a51f2e967b2" :step/math-academy-id 35525 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134842}} {:db/id 17592186134848 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135120 :tutorial/content "The following two vector fields behave either as a source or a sink. $$

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F.
